title: Every qcqs algebraic space has a finite finitely presented scheme cover
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] and let $X$ be an algebraic space over $S$ [def-trf-algebraic-space], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Assume $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated: it admits a surjective etale atlas from a quasi-compact scheme, and its absolute diagonal over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ is quasi-compact on affine scheme tests [def-sfb-stack-qcqs-morphism]. There exist an $S$-scheme $Y$ and a morphism $p:Y\to X$ that is surjective on field-valued point classes [def-a1-space-point-topology], finite, and of finite presentation. Finite means that every base change by an $S$-scheme $T\to X$ is a scheme finite over $T$ [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Finite presentation means quasi-compact, quasi-separated (quasi-compact relative diagonal), and locally of finite presentation after etale scheme charts [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. No Noetherian, separatedness, finite-type-over-$S$, or field hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 09YC (proposition-there-is-a-scheme-finite-over), clause (1), full arbitrary-base statement. This is the finite scheme cover used in Alper Theorem 4.3.1, final paragraph.

proof.text: By [lem-a1-space-etale-open-image], the assumed surjective etale atlas from a quasi-compact scheme implies that $|X|$ is quasi-compact. The cited statements ask that the absolute diagonal be quasi-compact on scheme tests, while the item assumes it on affine scheme tests. These agree: for a scheme $T$ with a map to $X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z}X$, let $W=T\times_{X\times X}X$. A quasi-compact open $V\subseteq T$ is a finite union of affine opens $V_k\subseteq V$, each an affine test, so $|W\times_TV|$ is the finite union of the quasi-compact images of the $|W\times_TV_k|$ and is quasi-compact. Thus $W\to T$ is quasi-compact. Hence the qcqs hypotheses of the cited statements hold over the given arbitrary scheme $S$.
Apply [lem-sfb-qcqs-space-integral-scheme-cover] to obtain an $S$-scheme $Z$ and a surjective integral $S$-morphism $q:Z\to X$. This uses only that $X$ is qcqs, not separated or Noetherian.

Apply [lem-sfb-integral-space-finite-presentation-limit] to $q$. It gives a small nonempty directed system $(Z_i\to X)$ of finite finitely presented morphisms, qcqs stages, affine transition maps and compatible $X$-maps $r_i:Z\to Z_i$ exhibiting $Z$ as their limit over $X$. It is also a limit over $S$: a compatible family of $S$-maps $W\to Z_i$ has a common composite $W\to X$, since any two indices have a common upper bound. Regard $W$ with that structure map and apply the limit property over $X$. Uniqueness over $S$ follows because any lift has that same composite to $X$, as seen after any one projection; there is an index because the system is nonempty.

The limit $Z$ is a scheme, so [lem-sfb-affine-space-limit-schematic-stage] applies to this small directed system of qcqs spaces over $S$ with affine transitions. Choose $i$ with $Y=Z_i$ a scheme, and let $p:Y\to X$ be its finite finitely presented structure morphism. It is surjective on point classes [def-a1-space-point-topology]: for any class $x$ of $X$, choose a field-valued representative of a class $z$ in $Z$ mapping to $x$ under $q$, and take its composite with $r_i$. This represents a class of $Y$ mapping to $x$, since $p\circ r_i=q$. Hence $Y,p$ satisfy every clause; surjectivity of $r_i$ is unnecessary.
